text: AST 101 (The Night Sky) and AST 102 (Stars and Galaxies) form a two-course introduction to astronomy at Example College for students with no physics background. AST 101 covers the celestial sphere, the Moon's phases and eclipses, the seasons, and light and telescopes. AST 102 covers measuring the stars, the lives of stars, galaxies and dark matter, and the expanding universe. Each course has four 75-minute lectures, one per week. The math is ratios and angles; a calculator is welcome.

Instructor: Dr. Alex Morgan. Office hours are Tuesdays and Thursdays after class, and by appointment. Questions about grades, extensions or personal circumstances go to Dr. Morgan directly, not to the course forum and not to Astra. Expect a reply within two working days.

The text is Open Astronomy Notes, free and written for these courses, posted on the course page as a PDF. You need a pencil, graph paper, a flashlight with a red filter or red cellophane for observing, and access to the sky. No telescope is required; the class telescopes are used at the observing night.

AST 101 and AST 102 are graded the same way: problem sets 35 percent, observing log 15 percent, midterm 20 percent, final exam 25 percent, in-class predictions and exit cards 5 percent. Predictions and exit cards are graded on completion only, never on whether the prediction was right. On problem sets and exams, reasoning and labeled diagrams earn most of the credit.

Each student has two late days per course, usable on problem sets with no explanation needed. A late day extends a deadline by 24 hours. Late days cannot be used on the last problem set of a course, because solutions are posted the day it is due. For anything beyond two late days, talk to Dr. Morgan before the deadline.

The observing log has five entries per course, each a short record of something you saw in the sky: the date, time, location, sky conditions, a sketch and two or three sentences. Entry 4 is the class observing night. A cloudy night counts if you say so and describe the clouds. An invented observation earns zero for the whole entry.

Each course has a midterm at the start of week 4, covering lectures 1 to 3, and a final exam in week 5 covering all four lectures. You may bring one handwritten page of notes, both sides. Expect to draw diagrams; a correct diagram earns partial credit even with a wrong final answer.

Astra is the course's AI tutor. It answers in Dr. Morgan's teaching style, grounds its answers in the course materials, and will not hand you the answers to graded problem sets; it gives hints and asks questions instead. You may use Astra on any assignment. It can be wrong: check what it tells you against the notes and the slides, and bring disagreements to office hours. Astra cannot change grades or deadlines.

Discussing problems with classmates is encouraged. Writing up someone else's solution, or copying an answer from any source, including an AI tool, is not. Your write-up must be your own reasoning in your own words. Observing log entries must be your own observations.
If you need accommodations, contact the college's accessibility office and let Dr. Morgan know in the first week. Observing activities have indoor alternatives for anyone who cannot attend at night.
